name: Radxa ROCK 5 ITX
summary: An ARM desktop, from boot to accelerated graphics.

Mali GPU acceleration with Mesa Panfrost
Rockchip MPP video decoding and analog audio
Intel AX210 Wi-Fi, including tested 802.11ax association

name: Radxa Cubie A7S
summary: A compact ARM desktop with PowerVR graphics and onboard wireless.
features: Bootable SD image and native Haiku desktop
PowerVR BXM-4-64 graphics through Mesa Zink: OpenGL 3.2 and OpenGL ES 3.1
Summit WebGL 1 and 2, with transform feedback support
Onboard AIC8800 Wi-Fi: 5 GHz WPA2, 802.11ac, DHCP and reconnection
Bluetooth Low Energy discovery; an A2DP audio implementation is available for testing

name: Radxa Dragon Q8B
summary: A Snapdragon desktop board with accelerated graphics, hardware video and two Ethernet ports, installed from the ARM64 ISO.
features: Installs from the ARM64 UEFI ISO onto the NVMe or an SD card, and boots from either
Adreno 690 graphics: Vulkan 1.3 with Mesa Turnip, OpenGL ES 3.2 and OpenGL through Zink, and WebGL 2 in Summit at 60 fps
Hardware H.264 and HEVC decoding and encoding on the Iris video codec, in airTime, Summit and MediaConverter
HDMI and both USB-C DisplayPort outputs as one desktop
Both Ethernet ports, Intel AX210 Wi-Fi 6, USB 3 and the SD card slot
Headphone and headset audio through the audio DSP, with HDMI and USB-C DisplayPort sound outputs

name: AMD Radeon Pro WX 5100
summary: An accelerated desktop on AMD: native display output, graphics and video.
features: Linux 6.18 amdgpu driver port with DRM, memory management and Display Core integrated into Haiku
Two 3840 × 2160 displays at 60 Hz, with scaling, arrangement and tested DisplayPort hotplug
Mesa radeonsi for OpenGL, OpenGL ES and Summit GPU compositing
RADV Vulkan 1.4, including windowed Vulkan through the in-process Wayland server
UVD H.264, HEVC and Main 10 decoding; VCE H.264/HEVC encoding
airTime 4K H.264 at 60 fps and HEVC Main 10 at 30 fps without drops in the recorded trials

name: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 / GTX 1080 Ti
summary: Native NVIDIA graphics with 2D acceleration, hardware video decoding and hardware H.264 encoding.
features: Native display output through nvidia_rm, with dual 4K monitors, per-display scaling and desktop arrangement
Mesa NVK Vulkan and Zink OpenGL 4.5 on the tested Pascal cards

2D acceleration on the card's 2D engine: fills, inverts, spans and blits for full-screen programs, and app_server's copies to the screen, where a 4K copy takes 2.9 ms on the engine against 7.1 ms on the CPU
NVDEC hardware H.264 decoding through a system media add-on: tested GTX 1080 Ti streams match FFmpeg software decoding byte for byte
NVDEC decoded the recorded 1080p test at 232 frames per second; NVPlay provides playback with audio and seeking
NVENC hardware H.264 encoding in MediaConverter, tested on the GTX 1070: a 10½-minute 1080p film encoded at 254 frames per second (8.5× real time) and decoded back at 43.8 dB PSNR
Tested NVENC sizes from 33×32 to 4096×4096, quality and average-bit-rate modes, DVD, Blu-ray, VP9 and 10-bit sources, and six conversions at once
NVENC must pass an encode/decode self-test for each card and format before use; formats and sizes it cannot encode go to the CPU, and MediaConverter says so
limits: NVENC encodes H.264 with I and P pictures only; B-frame encoding is not implemented. On Pascal, H.265 is encoded on the CPU: the engine encodes H.265 I pictures but rejects P pictures, so H.265 fails the self-test. AV1 encoding uses the CPU, including on Ada and Blackwell. Other NVIDIA generations run the same NVENC code but have not been tested; the self-test decides whether each format uses the GPU. Verified NVDEC coverage is progressive 8-bit 4:2:0 H.264; interlaced, 4:2:2 and higher-bit-depth streams are unsupported and may fail to play instead of falling back. The 2D engine copies finished frames to the screen; app_server still draws its anti-aliased content on the CPU, so drawing throughput is largely unchanged. These results describe the Pascal workstation configuration, not every NVIDIA GPU.

name: Framework Laptop 13
chip: x86-64 · AMD Radeon 760M · Ryzen AI 5 340 with Radeon 840M
summary: AMD graphics, Thunderbolt docks, sleep and a working touchpad on a high-density laptop desktop.
features: Native desktop output through amdgpu_drm
Ryzen AI 5 340 with Radeon 840M: working properly, with every feature listed here
Scaled desktop and native application windows; the Craft ports have been checked at 175% density
MediaConverter detects the Radeon 760M and offers hardware H.264 encoding
Suspend and resume: closing the lid puts the laptop to sleep (suspend to idle, S0ix) and opening it wakes it again; Power preferences choose what the lid does
The built-in touchpad works, which it does not on stock Haiku: a precision touchpad over I2C HID, with tap to click and smooth two-finger scrolling

Thunderbolt and USB4: air/OS runs its own connection manager for the USB-C ports, carrying USB 3, DisplayPort and PCIe to docks and devices, which then show up as ordinary USB devices, monitors and PCI devices; plugging and unplugging works on chained devices too
Tested with a Lenovo ThinkPad Thunderbolt 4 dock: its monitors, USB devices, Ethernet and internal PCIe switch all work, with the dock attached at boot or unplugged and replugged while running
A second 4K monitor on the dock's HDMI port, behind its MST hub, comes up beside the first
limits: These are the tested Radeon 760M and Ryzen AI 5 340 (Radeon 840M) configurations, not a claim about every Framework model. Thunderbolt has been tested with one dock on the Ryzen AI 5 340; NVMe enclosures and external GPUs use the same PCIe tunnels but have not been tried. Not done yet for Thunderbolt: host-to-host networking, firmware updates for docks and devices, low-power link states, DisplayPort bandwidth allocation mode, and keeping Thunderbolt devices across sleep. See the driver source and current package notes for device-specific coverage.
